lessons.title: Integrated final assessment: choosing the right tool
lessons.description: Eleven scenario questions that mix all three parts — pick the method, justify it, compute it, interpret it.
objectives: Select the mathematical concept that fits a structured data science or machine learning question
Carry the calculation through correctly and interpret the result in context
Spot the classic misreading (wrong sign, standard deviation vs standard error, reversed conditional)
lessons.objectivesLead: By the end of this assessment you can:
lessons.body:
The final assessment is worth 50% of the course and asks for something different from the topic quizzes: you are given a **situation** and must decide which tool applies, apply it, and say what the answer means. The questions below are a full-length rehearsal covering LO.2–LO.10.

## Choosing the tool

| The question sounds like… | Reach for… | Part |
|---|---|---|
| "How many solutions / can this system be solved?" | Augmented matrix, row reduction, rank | I |
| "Can I undo this transformation?" | Determinant ≠ 0, inverse | I |
| "Which directions does this matrix stretch or preserve?" | Eigenvalues and eigenvectors | I |
| "How fast does the output change when I nudge an input?" | Derivative, chain rule, marginal effect | II |
| "How do I adjust several parameters to lower the loss?" | Gradient, gradient descent | II |
| "How likely is X given that I observed Y?" | Conditional probability, Bayes' rule | III |
| "What is the typical value and spread of a random quantity?" | Expectation, variance | III |
| "How do two quantities move together?" | Covariance, correlation, conditional expectation | III |
| "How much can I trust this sample average?" | Sampling distribution, CLT, standard error, confidence interval | III |

> [!meo] Before computing, write one sentence naming the object you are asked for (a probability, a rate of change, a direction, an interval). Most lost marks come from answering a neighbouring question correctly.

> [!canh-bao] Time yourself: the quiz is built for about 40 minutes. Do the calculations on paper first; the answer check appears only after you commit.
summary: Decide first what is being asked, then choose the method.
Check each result for plausibility: probabilities in [0,1], variances non-negative, descent steps that lower the loss.
The same mathematical objects (matrices, gradients, distributions) appear in every part — the final assessment is about moving between them.

questions.prompt: You fit the line $y=a+bx$ to the points $(1,2)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,5)$ by solving the normal equations $X^TX\,\beta=X^Ty$ with $\beta=(a,b)^T$. What is the slope $b$? (Give a decimal or a fraction.)
questions.explanation: $X^TX=\begin{bmatrix}3&6\\6&14\end{bmatrix}$ and $X^Ty=\begin{bmatrix}10\\23\end{bmatrix}$. Row-reduce (or use the inverse, $\det=6$): $a=\tfrac13$, $b=\tfrac32$. Check the residuals: the fitted values $\tfrac{11}{6},\tfrac{20}{6},\tfrac{29}{6}$ are close to $2,3,5$.

questions.prompt: A data set has covariance matrix $\Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$. Which statement about the direction of **maximum variance** is correct?
questions.explanation: $\det(\Sigma-\lambda I)=(2-\lambda)^2-1=0$ gives $\lambda=3$ and $\lambda=1$. For $\lambda=3$: $(\Sigma-3I)v=0$ gives $v=(1,1)$. The variance along an eigenvector equals its eigenvalue, so the share is $3/(3+1)=75\%$. The equal diagonal entries only mean the two axes have equal variance; the correlation $\Sigma_{12}=1$ tilts the best direction by $45^\circ$.

options.label: It is the eigenvector for the eigenvalue $3$, i.e. the direction $(1,1)/\sqrt2$, and it carries $75\%$ of the total variance.
It is the eigenvector for the eigenvalue $1$, i.e. $(1,-1)/\sqrt2$, and it carries $25\%$ of the total variance.
It is the first coordinate axis $(1,0)$, because $\Sigma_{11}=2$ is the largest diagonal entry.
There is no unique direction, because the two variances are equal.

questions.prompt: The loss is $L(w_1,w_2)=w_1^2+3w_2^2$. Starting at $w=(2,1)$, one gradient-descent step with learning rate $\eta=0.1$ gives which point?
questions.explanation: $\nabla L=(2w_1,\,6w_2)=(4,6)$ at $(2,1)$. Descent moves **against** the gradient: $w\leftarrow w-\eta\nabla L=(2-0.4,\,1-0.6)=(1.6,\,0.4)$. Adding the gradient would climb the hill; using the wrong partial derivative (e.g. $3w_2$ instead of $6w_2$) gives $(1.8,0.7)$.

questions.prompt: The logistic function is $\sigma(z)=\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$. What is $\sigma'(0)$?
questions.explanation: By the chain rule $\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)\,(1-\sigma(z))$. At $z=0$, $\sigma(0)=\tfrac12$ so $\sigma'(0)=\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac14$. The value $0.5$ is $\sigma(0)$ itself, not its slope.

questions.prompt: A spam filter: $20\%$ of mail is spam. The word "prize" appears in $60\%$ of spam and $10\%$ of non-spam. An email contains "prize". What is $P(\text{spam}\mid\text{prize})$?
questions.explanation: Bayes: $\dfrac{0.6\cdot0.2}{0.6\cdot0.2+0.1\cdot0.8}=\dfrac{0.12}{0.20}=0.60$. $0.12$ is only the numerator (the joint probability); $0.6$ is $P(\text{prize}\mid\text{spam})$, which is a different conditional.
$\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)$: the shift $-2$ does not change spread and the factor $3$ is squared, so $9\cdot4=36$. (Also $E[Y]=3\cdot1-2=1$.)

questions.prompt: A sample of $n=100$ values has mean $\bar x=50$ and the population standard deviation is known to be $\sigma=15$. Which is the $95\%$ confidence interval for the mean, and how should it be read?
questions.explanation: The standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n=15/10=1.5$, so the margin is $1.96\cdot1.5\approx2.94$ and the interval is $[47.06,52.94]$. $\mu$ is a fixed number; the $95\%$ describes the **procedure**, not this one interval. Using $\sigma=15$ instead of the standard error $1.5$ describes the spread of individual values, not the uncertainty of the mean.

options.label: $[47.06,\ 52.94]$ — if we repeated the sampling many times, about $95\%$ of intervals built this way would contain $\mu$.
$[47.06,\ 52.94]$ — there is a $95\%$ probability that $\mu$ lies in this particular interval.
$[35.0,\ 65.0]$ — the margin is $\sigma$ and the interval does not depend on $n$.

questions.prompt: You flip a coin $10$ times and see $7$ heads. What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of the probability of heads?
questions.explanation: The likelihood $p^7(1-p)^3$ is maximised where its derivative of the log vanishes: $7/p-3/(1-p)=0$, so $\hat p=7/10$.

questions.prompt: Observations are i.i.d. with variance $\sigma^2=10$. The estimator $\tilde S^2=\dfrac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2$ is computed from samples of size $n=5$. What is $E[\tilde S^2]$?
questions.explanation: Dividing by $n$ instead of $n-1$ gives $E[\tilde S^2]=\dfrac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2=\dfrac45\cdot10=8$. The estimator is biased low by $2$; dividing by $n-1$ removes the bias.

questions.prompt: If two random variables are uncorrelated ($\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0$), they must be independent.
questions.explanation: False. Independence implies zero covariance, not the other way round. Take $X$ symmetric about $0$ and $Y=X^2$: $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=E[X^3]-E[X]E[X^2]=0$, yet $Y$ is completely determined by $X$.

questions.prompt: Match each data-science task with the mathematical tool from this course that answers it.

pairs.left: Does a system of equations have a unique solution?
Minimise a differentiable loss over parameters
Probability of a disease given a positive test
Directions a covariance matrix stretches the data most

questions.explanation: Choosing the right tool is learning outcome LO.10. Each pairing follows from the question being asked: existence/uniqueness → rank; "how do I improve parameters" → gradient; reversing a conditional → Bayes; precision of an estimate → standard error; principal directions → eigen-decomposition.

misconceptions.name: Picking the smallest eigenvalue
misconceptions.description: Treats the eigenvector of the smallest eigenvalue as the direction of maximum variance, or mixes up which eigenvalue measures how much spread lies along its eigenvector.

misconceptions.name: Reading the direction off the diagonal
misconceptions.description: Assumes the direction of maximum variance is a coordinate axis, or that equal variances mean no preferred direction, ignoring the off-diagonal covariance.

misconceptions.name: Wrong sign in the update
misconceptions.description: Adds the gradient instead of subtracting it, or subtracts without multiplying by the learning rate.

misconceptions.name: Slipping on a partial derivative
misconceptions.description: Differentiates one coordinate with the wrong rule (for example $3w_2$ instead of $6w_2$) when assembling the gradient.

misconceptions.name: Confusing a function with its derivative
misconceptions.description: Reports $\sigma(0)$ (the value) when asked for $\sigma'(0)$ (the slope).

misconceptions.name: Dropping the denominator or the prior
misconceptions.description: Reports the joint probability (numerator of Bayes' rule) or the prior as if it were the posterior.

misconceptions.name: Reversing the conditional
misconceptions.description: Treats $P(\text{word}\mid\text{spam})$ as if it were $P(\text{spam}\mid\text{word})$ or computes a ratio that mixes the two.

misconceptions.name: Probability statement about a fixed interval
misconceptions.description: Says there is a $95\%$ probability that $\mu$ is inside this particular computed interval.

misconceptions.name: Standard deviation instead of standard error
misconceptions.description: Uses $\sigma$ (spread of individual observations) where the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$ (spread of the sample mean) belongs.

feedbackTemplates.body: The variance along an eigenvector of the covariance matrix **equals its eigenvalue**, so the largest eigenvalue marks the direction of greatest spread. Recompute both eigenvalues and compare.
The off-diagonal entry is the covariance between the variables and tilts the principal axis away from the coordinate axes. Always find eigenvectors; do not read the answer off the diagonal.
The gradient points uphill (direction of steepest **increase**). To reduce the loss move the opposite way: $w \leftarrow w - \eta\nabla L$.
Take each partial derivative separately, treating the other variable as a constant: $\partial/\partial w_2\,(3w_2^2)=6w_2$.
Read the question for the quantity being asked: $\sigma(0)=0.5$ but the slope is $\sigma(0)(1-\sigma(0))=0.25$.

The posterior divides by the **total** probability of the evidence: $P(\text{spam}\mid\text{word})=P(\text{word}\mid\text{spam})P(\text{spam})/P(\text{word})$, with $P(\text{word})$ from the law of total probability.
$P(A\mid B)$ and $P(B\mid A)$ are different numbers; Bayes' rule is exactly the bridge between them, and it needs the prior.
$\mu$ is fixed and the interval is already computed, so it either contains $\mu$ or not. The $95\%$ is the long-run proportion of intervals built this way that capture $\mu$.
The mean of $n$ observations varies less than a single observation: its standard deviation is $\sigma/\sqrt n$. A confidence interval for $\mu$ must use that.
Covariance measures only **linear** association. $Y=X^2$ with $X$ symmetric about $0$ has zero covariance but is fully dependent on $X$.
